analysis.one_liner: Strips tax exemption from nonprofit hospitals that fail to provide charity care to low-income uninsured patients.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: its sponsor, the chairman of the committee it was sent to, introduced it with no cosponsors three weeks before Congress ended, and the committee took no action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required tax-exempt hospitals to have and follow policies for providing medically necessary care to low-income uninsured people, charged them $1,000 each time they refused such care, capped what they could bill patients earning under the poverty line at $25 per visit, and required them to disclose their charity-care policies and price lists publicly. A hospital that lost its tax-exempt status would also lose its ability to receive tax-deductible donations. Hospitals that overcharged low-income uninsured patients would owe a tax of three times the excess amount.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income uninsured patients — those earning up to 200% of the poverty line — who seek care at tax-exempt hospitals. They would be guaranteed written policies on charity care, capped charges (a $25-per-visit maximum for households under the poverty line), and public price disclosure instead of facing full uninsured billing rates.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured patients earning under twice the poverty line

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals could lose their federal tax exemption unless they adopted and operated under policies providing and charging for medically necessary care to low-income uninsured patients.

A hospital that turned away a low-income uninsured patient seeking an in-person visit would owe a $1,000 excise tax for each failure, and one that overcharged such a patient would owe three times the excess amount.
For patients with household income at or below the poverty line, the maximum allowable charge for medically necessary care would be $25 per visit.

Hospitals would have to tell patients about their charity-care policies during admission and billing, and publish their charity-care policies and average prices actually paid for each procedure by insurer, self-pay, and government programs.

analysis.who_pays: Tax-exempt hospitals and teaching hospitals, which would face new excise taxes, compliance costs, capped revenue from low-income uninsured patients, and the possible loss of their tax exemption — which would also make donations to them non-deductible.

drawbacks.text: The bill excluded from its protections anyone eligible for government-sponsored insurance, so patients eligible for Medicaid or Medicare but not enrolled would not have qualified for the capped charges or charity-care guarantees.

Hospitals would bear real administrative costs: income and asset documentation for patients, published price lists, and per-failure penalties of $1,000, which hospital groups would argue could strain facilities serving many low-income patients and have little effect on hospitals in wealthier areas.
The $25-per-visit cap for patients under the poverty line is a fixed amount unrelated to the actual cost of care, which hospitals would argue forces them to absorb a loss on every such visit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For low-income uninsured patients, the benefit is concrete: enforceable charity-care policies, sharply capped bills, and public price information from institutions that currently enjoy a large tax subsidy partly in exchange for community benefit. The cost falls almost entirely on tax-exempt hospitals and their donors, though a fair objection is that the design was blunt — fixed dollar penalties and a flat $25 visit cap regardless of actual costs, and no protection for patients eligible for, but not enrolled in, government insurance. The bill was a pressure mechanism as much as a program.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and died there; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Thomas, the chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, introduced the bill on December 8, 2006, and referred it to his own committee.
The bill's only recorded actions are its introduction and referral to committee; nothing further happened before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tax-exempt hospitals came out ahead: they faced no new charity-care requirements, billing caps, or disclosure rules, and kept their tax exemption and the tax deductibility of donations to them.

for.name: Rep. Bill Thomas
for.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 8, 2006, three and a half weeks before the end of the 109th Congress, and referred it to the Ways and Means Committee he chaired.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax exemption and excise taxes
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record; the sponsor was a Republican committee chairman acting days before the session ended.

industries.note: These hospitals hold a federal tax exemption whose traditional rationale includes providing charity care, but they bill uninsured low-income patients at full rates. The bill would have taxed or stripped the exemption from hospitals that refused medically necessary care to such patients, capped their charges, and forced price disclosure — a direct cost to the industry and a direct gain for uninsured patients.

industries.industry: Charitable and philanthropic donors to hospitals
industries.note: Donations to a hospital that lost its 501(c)(3) status under the bill would no longer be tax-deductible, which hospitals would argue could reduce charitable giving that funds care.
